Data Vault Foundations Updates
Law as of 20 November 2026

Updates

This site was first published in March 2026. The law it teaches has moved since: on 27 July 2026 the EU amended the AI Act. On 20 November 2026 the regulation chapters were checked again against the official texts. This page lists every change that check produced. For each one you can read what the page said before, what it says now, and where the law says so.

How to read this page

Nothing on this site is rewritten silently. In the chapters, every changed passage carries an Updated mark and keeps the earlier text next to it. It is the rule a Data Vault follows: new rows are added with their date, old rows stay.

Chapter 5 · Compliance and GDPR4 updates

Updated 20 Nov 2026The law changed on 27 July 2026

The bias-testing exception moved from Article 10(5) to Article 4a, and now reaches deployers

Before

Article 10(5) creates a limited exception to GDPR's prohibition on processing special category data. Providers of high-risk AI may process this data for bias detection and correction.

Now

Article 4a creates the exception. Until July 2026 it was Article 10(5) and covered only providers of high-risk AI. The amendment moved it to Article 4a and opened it, on the same six conditions, to deployers of high-risk AI and to providers and deployers of other AI systems and models. Deletion is due once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever comes first.

Source
  • AI Act, consolidated text of 27 July 2026 (EUR-Lex 02024R1689-20260727) Art. 4a
  • Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, OJ L of 24 July 2026 Art. 1(6) inserts Art. 4a; Art. 1(9)(b) deletes Art. 10(5)
See it in chapter 5 →

Chapter 7 · EU Regulations6 updates

Updated 20 Nov 2026Correction

The ePrivacy Regulation was not withdrawn in February 2025: that was the announcement

Before

The ePrivacy Regulation was formally withdrawn by the EU Commission in February 2025.

Now

It was withdrawn in 2025, in three steps. On 11 February 2025 the Commission announced that it intended to withdraw the proposal. On 16 July 2025 it approved the withdrawal. On 6 October 2025 the withdrawal was published in the Official Journal. The ePrivacy Directive of 2002 is still in force.

Source
  • Withdrawal of Commission proposals, OJ C/2025/5423 of 6 October 2025 closing sentence: approved at the 2533rd meeting, 16 July 2025
  • Commission Work Programme 2025, COM(2025) 45 final, Annex IV item 29
See it in chapter 7 →

Where: ePrivacy section, layer 4; comparison table; "On ePrivacy" quote; fold-out note; Exercise 2, statement 3

Updated 20 Nov 2026Events since publication

The Digital Omnibus on data is still a proposal

Before

The Commission proposed a "Digital Omnibus" package in late 2025 that may fold some ePrivacy territory into a broader legislative revision. Whether this succeeds is genuinely uncertain.

Now

The proposal (COM(2025) 837, 19 November 2025) would move the cookie rules for personal data into the GDPR. It is not law. The Council agreed its negotiating position on 21 October 2026, and that position keeps the cookie rules in the ePrivacy Directive. The European Parliament has not adopted a position, so talks between the two have not started. The separate Digital Omnibus on AI did become law (see chapter 9).

Source
  • Digital Omnibus proposal, COM(2025) 837 final Art. 5 and new GDPR Art. 88a
  • Council press release of 21 October 2026 "maintains the rules on cookies ... under the e-privacy directive"
  • European Parliament, procedure file 2025/0360(COD) status: awaiting committee decision

Updated 20 Nov 2026Correction

"In force" and "applies" are two different dates

Before

A table row labelled "In force" gave May 2018 (GDPR), Sep 2025 (Data Act) and Jan 2025 (DORA). A note said the Data Governance Act was "in force Sep 2023" and the Data Act "in force Sep 2025".

Now

The row is labelled "Applies since". Those are the dates from which the rules must be followed. Updated 20 Nov 2026Correction

DORA article numbers

Before

Article 6: register of ICT assets. Article 17: classify and report incidents. Article 25: testing, including TLPT. "The CTPP framework (Articles 28-44)". "DORA Art. 6" in the lineage table.

Now

Article 8 (identification) is the duty to identify and document ICT assets and their dependencies; Article 6 is the overall risk framework. Incidents: Articles 17 to 19 (reporting is Article 19). Testing: Articles 24 to 26 (threat-led penetration testing is Article 26). The oversight framework for critical providers is Articles 31 to 44; Articles 28 to 30 are the general third-party risk rules.

Source
  • DORA, Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 Arts. 6, 8, 17-19, 24-26, 28-44

Updated 20 Nov 2026Events since publication

EU-US Data Privacy Framework: still valid; first challenge dismissed, appeal pending

Before

Currently valid for certified US organizations. "Schrems III?": NOYB has indicated it will challenge the DPF. Status: Challenge Expected.

Now

The framework is still valid on 20 November 2026. On 3 September 2025 the EU General Court dismissed the first challenge (T-553/23, Latombe v Commission). The appeal to the Court of Justice (C-703/25 P, lodged 31 October 2025) is pending: no Advocate General opinion and no judgment yet. NOYB has not filed a case so far; on 29 June 2026 it announced that it would, after the US Supreme Court ruled in Trump v. Slaughter that the President may dismiss FTC commissioners. On 31 July 2026 the European Data Protection Board asked the Commission to assess whether that ruling affects the framework.

Source
  • Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1795 (EU-US Data Privacy Framework) in force
  • General Court, judgment of 3 September 2025, T-553/23 Latombe v Commission operative part: "Dismisses the action"
  • Court of Justice, case C-703/25 P, register entry read on 20 November 2026 status: pending
  • US Supreme Court, Trump v. Slaughter, No. 25-332, 29 June 2026 syllabus
  • European Data Protection Board, letter to the Commission of 31 July 2026
  • noyb, statement of 29 June 2026 "will also file a lawsuit in the coming weeks"

Chapter 9 · AI Act and Data Vault15 updates

Updated 20 Nov 2026Correction

Social scoring is banned for everyone, not only for governments

Before

Social scoring by a government (rating citizens' behavior to restrict services) is banned outright. Quiz feedback said the Act bans social scoring "by public authorities".

Now

The ban in Article 5(1)(c) covers any AI system that scores people on their social behaviour or personal traits and then treats them worse in an unrelated setting or out of proportion. It applies to public bodies and private companies alike. The feedback texts of Exercise 1 were corrected to match.

Source
  • AI Act, consolidated text of 27 July 2026 (EUR-Lex 02024R1689-20260727) Art. 5(1)(c)

Updated 20 Nov 2026The law changed on 27 July 2026

The Digital Omnibus on AI is law

Before

Digital Omnibus proposal (Nov 2025): the Commission proposed delaying Annex III enforcement by up to 16 months. Not yet adopted. Clients are in limbo: the enforcement timeline is shifting.

Now

Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 was published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on 27 July 2026. Germany's implementing law (KI-MIG) is in force

Before

Germany's Federal Cabinet approved the KI-MIG in February 2026, designating the Bundesnetzagentur as primary AI market surveillance authority, though the law is still completing its parliamentary process.

Now

The Bundestag passed the law on 11 June 2026. It was published on 28 July 2026 and has applied since 29 July 2026. Updated 20 Nov 2026The law changed on 27 July 2026

Article 10(5) was deleted; the rule is now Article 4a and reaches deployers

Before

Article 10(5) opens a narrow door: you can process special category data for bias detection. Article 10(5) is the legal basis.

Now

Article 4a(1) carries the same six conditions that Article 10(5) had, for providers of high-risk systems. Article 4a(2) opens the same door, on the same conditions, to deployers of high-risk systems and to providers and deployers of other AI systems and models, and creates no duty to run such tests. Recital 9 of the amending regulation ties the exception to GDPR Art. 9(2)(g); whether it can stand alone as a legal basis is still debated among scholars.

Source
  • AI Act, consolidated text of 27 July 2026 (EUR-Lex 02024R1689-20260727) Art. 4a; Art. 10(1) and (6)
  • Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, OJ L of 24 July 2026 Art. 1(6); Art. 1(9)(b); recital 9
See it in chapter 9 →

Where: Article 10, layer 4; dual compliance, card 1

Updated 20 Nov 2026The law changed on 27 July 2026

AI literacy (Article 4) was reworded

Before

Applies to all AI systems. Already in effect since Feb 2025. No standalone fine, but non-compliance is an aggravating factor. For BI consultants, understanding the AI Act is a legal obligation.

Now

Providers and deployers must take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff and of others who operate AI on their behalf. The text now says this does not require guaranteeing any specific level of AI literacy for any individual. Article 99 sets no fine of its own for Article 4. The sentence about an "aggravating factor" was removed: the Act does not say that. The sentence that called AI Act knowledge a legal obligation for consultants was softened: the duty in Article 4 falls on providers and deployers.

Source
  • AI Act, consolidated text of 27 July 2026 (EUR-Lex 02024R1689-20260727) Art. 4; Art. 99
  • Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, OJ L of 24 July 2026 Art. 1(5)
See it in chapter 9 →

Checked and left as it was

These statements were checked against the same sources on 20 November 2026 and are still right.

  • Ch. 9 The AI Act is Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 and entered into force on 1 August 2024. Art. 113, first paragraph
  • Ch. 9 Fines: up to EUR 35 million or 7% for banned practices; EUR 15 million or 3%; EUR 7.5 million or 1% for incorrect information. Art. 99(3) to (5)
  • Ch. 9 Serious incidents: report within 15 days; 2 days for a widespread infringement or a serious disruption of critical infrastructure. (Also in the Act: 10 days where a person has died.) Art. 73(2) to (4)
  • Ch. 9 The eight Annex III areas and the examples given for each, including targeted job advertising under employment and credit scoring under essential services. Annex III, points 1 to 8
  • Ch. 9 Obligations for general-purpose AI models apply since 2 August 2025; models already on the market have until 2 August 2027. Art. 113, third paragraph, point (b); Art. 111(3)
  • Ch. 9 Article 10(6): for systems that are not trained on data, the data rules apply to the testing data sets only. Art. 10(6)
  • Ch. 7 DORA applies from 17 January 2025 and entered into force in January 2023. Art. 64
  • Ch. 7 Data Act: most rules apply from 12 September 2025; the design duty for new connected products from 12 September 2026; cloud switching is Articles 23 to 31; fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory terms are in Article 8. Art. 50; Art. 8(1); Chapter VI
  • Ch. 5 GDPR fines: up to EUR 20 million or 4% (Art. 83(5)); EUR 10 million or 2% (Art. 83(4)). Applies since 25 May 2018. Art. 83(4) and (5); Art. 99
  • Ch. 8 Schrems I (C-362/14, 6 October 2015) struck down Safe Harbour; Schrems II (C-311/18, 16 July 2020) struck down Privacy Shield and kept standard contractual clauses. C-311/18 on EUR-Lex; Schrems I is C-362/14
  • Ch. 8 The CLOUD Act (2018) reaches data in a provider's "possession, custody, or control" wherever it is stored. 18 U.S.C. § 2713
  • Ch. 8 Whether the EU-based sovereign cloud offerings are out of reach of the CLOUD Act has not been tested in an EU court: no ruling was found on 20 November 2026. no EU court ruling on this point was found
  • Ch. 8 Japan's adequacy decision covers private-sector business operators; the US decision covers certified organisations only. Decision (EU) 2019/419, Art. 1(1); US: Commission list

This is a learning site, not legal advice. The official texts are on EUR-Lex; where this site and the Official Journal differ, the Official Journal is right. Back to the chapters
